name: Seedfall

detectability.signature: Dense organic particulate field; amino acid spectral lines; visible as a pale green-gold haze with denser clumps drifting on solar wind

proximity: Ship sensors detect increasing concentration of organic particles
Spores adhere to hull surfaces and begin dormant colonization of exterior
Air filtration systems flag biological contaminants if any external intake is active
contact: Spore density sufficient to reduce visibility and coat all external surfaces
Hull micro-fractures and port seals infiltrated by spore tendrils seeking atmosphere
Bioluminescent reaction when spores contact ship waste heat—hull glows faint green
prolonged_exposure: Spore infiltration of interior atmosphere if hull integrity is less than perfect
Exterior hull surfaces develop visible fungal-analog growth consuming hull coatings
Ship systems with organic components experience accelerated degradation

age: estimated 200-400 million years of continuous dispersal

behavior.cycle: Spore density fluctuates with local stellar wind pressure on a 7-day period

phenomena: Spores or microorganisms in surrounding space visible as green-gold particulate haze
Bioluminescent displays when spores contact heat sources
Organic signatures on sensors at increasing concentration toward center
Pheromone-like chemical signatures affecting crew alertness and appetite
hazards: Contamination by exotic organisms degrading hull coatings and seals
Life support consumption by organisms if spores breach interior atmosphere
Crew behavioral changes from pheromone-like exposure—increased appetite, drowsiness
opportunities: Unique biological compounds—spore cell walls contain a polymer stronger than spider silk
Data on extremophile biology and panspermia mechanisms
Agricultural applications—several spore-derived compounds accelerate Terran crop growth
known_incidents: The colony transport Meadowlark transited Seedfall in 2578 with imperfect hull seals; within weeks, interior gardens exploded with growth from spore contamination, producing edible fungal structures that the colonists eventually cultivated intentionally.

Xenobiologist Dr. Tomas Ren spent four months collecting samples in 2649 and identified over 3,400 distinct spore species, concluding that Seedfall represents an entire ecosystem dispersed across interstellar space.
description: Seedfall is a cloud of life drifting through the void. Spanning 3.2 AU of space, it manifests as a pale green-gold haze—dense enough to be visible on approach, thick enough to coat a ship's hull within hours of entry. Spectral analysis confirms what the eye suspects: the cloud is composed of trillions upon trillions of biological spores, each one a dormant seed waiting for the right conditions to germinate. They ride the stellar wind in clumps and filaments, glowing faintly green when they encounter waste heat, as if responding to the warmth of a living ship with something uncomfortably like recognition.

The spores are tenacious, resourceful, and patient. They adhere to any surface and begin probing for entry points—micro-fractures in hull plating, imperfect seals around ports and hatches, any gap that might lead to atmosphere and warmth. Ships with compromised hulls learn quickly what the spores can do: within days of interior breach, fungal-analog structures bloom in warm, humid spaces, consuming organic hull coatings and producing fruiting bodies that release secondary spores adapted to the ship's internal environment. The process is not aggressive so much as relentless—the spores are simply doing what billions of years of evolution designed them to do.

Dr. Ren's census of 3,400 distinct species within Seedfall suggests that the cloud is not a single organism but an entire dispersed ecosystem—predators, prey, decomposers, and symbionts all reduced to spore form and scattered across astronomical distances. The implication is staggering: somewhere, presumably, there is a source world where these organisms exist in their full, non-dormant forms. No such world has been identified. The spores' dispersal age of 200 to 400 million years means the source could be anywhere within a considerable volume of the galaxy, or could no longer exist at all.

Seedfall occupies a growing niche in the galactic economy. The Meadowlark incident proved that some spore species are not only harmless but useful—the edible fungal structures have become a staple crop on three colony worlds. Spore-derived polymers outperform synthetic alternatives in tensile strength, and agricultural compounds extracted from the cloud have measurably improved yields on dozens of farming planets. Harvesting operations work the cloud's periphery, scooping spores in filtered intakes and processing them in sealed laboratories. The work is straightforward but carries a persistent unease: every biologist who studies Seedfall eventually asks the same question. If these are seeds, what are they meant to grow into?
